summary.countingConvention: Overlapping review bundles: short lessons + questions + glossary entries + formula cards. Corrections are recorded edit groups, including source and alias corrections; no atomic-fact count is claimed.

corrections: Inherited glossary definitions now distinguish IRIW with explicitly ordered readers and revised multicopy-atomic Arm from weaker or unordered cases; added a separate negative-model entry so non-MCA never opens the positive definition.

Qualified C/C++ acquire/release publication, compiler versus hardware barriers, exclusive-store spurious failure, restrict access contracts, per-object relaxed atomics, and writeback versus coherence visibility.

Removed integer-reassociation overstatement: signed C overflow is undefined; fixed-width unsigned addition wraps. Qualified reductions, if-conversion, masks, gathered accesses and target-specific compiler decisions.
Separated GFLOP and TFLOP operation counts from rates, A100 from H100, and C volatile from Java volatile; retained stable existing glossary IDs and gave new concepts distinct IDs.

Qualified GPU occupancy, divergence timing, sector versus DRAM transfers, shared/global/managed-memory visibility, tensor-core precision and host-memory access. GPU examples remain explicitly hypothetical where appropriate.

Qualified roofline intensity/ridge as model ceilings rather than guaranteed actual bottlenecks. Top-down slot percentages, sampling events and monotonic-clock behaviour now carry their correct limits.

Removed unsupported generic pipeline packet-rate/latency, debug-build slowdown and Rosetta hardware/performance claims from glossary definitions. Added stated packet-rate, batching, bfloat16 and weight-reuse worked context where short-unit questions require it.

Added meaningful code comments, complete symbolic grouping and local definitions; removed inline symbolic equations from active prose/options and corrected question explanation qualifications without changing any original answer key.

gaps: No CUDA-capable GPU, FPGA or TPU hardware is available. CUDA indexing and divergence fragments were exercised only through labelled CPU simulations; launch syntax/runtime synchronisation and actual device performance were not executed.

Linux perf 6.12.111 installed in an ephemeral container. Real stat and record attempts fail with existing perf_event_open EPERM; report correctly sees no data. No permissions were changed. Displayed counter numbers and timing diagrams are illustrative, never measurements from this host.

No physical x86 machine memory-order experiment was performed. AVX compiled x86-64 code ran through Rosetta on an arm64 host. Finite SC/TSO models and fetched ISA/language primary contracts support the ordering teaching; they are not exhaustive proofs of every concurrent program.

Existing scope exclusions are retained: generic latency/energy/cost ratios, exhaustive MISD products and hardware-generation configuration catalogues, Rosetta implementation/performance attribution and universal Linux spinlock/PMU resource catalogues.

The independent verifier reran exact CPU examples and wrote additional finite models; this does not provide CUDA launch execution, physical-GPU timing, FPGA timing closure, TPU execution or unrestricted PMU measurements. Existing perf EPERM was respected; no permission change or retry was attempted.

A universal perf sampling default, PMU overhead figure and CPU miss-buffer count: these depend on tool version, permissions, processor and workload and were not reliably established for a single stated target.

before.definition: Single instruction, multiple threads: NVIDIA's name for its GPU execution model. You write scalar code for one thread; the hardware groups threads into 32-thread warps and issues each instruction to the warp's active threads.

after.definition: Single instruction, multiple threads: NVIDIA's name for its GPU execution model. You write scalar code for one thread; the hardware groups threads into 32-thread warps and issues each instruction to the warp's active threads.

before.definition: The 256-bit x86 SIMD registers introduced with AVX, named ymm0, ymm1 and so on. The lower 128 bits of each are the SSE xmm register; AVX-512 extends them to the 512-bit zmm registers.

after.definition: XMM, YMM and ZMM name 128-bit, 256-bit and 512-bit x86 vector-register views on targets supporting the corresponding extensions. Where the views exist for the same register number, XMM is the low 128 bits of YMM and YMM is the low 256 bits of ZMM. A YMM register itself is 256 bits, not 128 or 512 bits.

before.definition: A memory-model constraint on the propagation order in which observers see writes. Other-multi-copy atomicity permits an issuing thread to read its own buffered write early while constraining propagation to other observers; it is not a claim of zero physical propagation time.

after.definition: A memory-model constraint on the propagation order in which observers see writes. Other-multi-copy atomicity permits an issuing thread to read its own buffered write early while constraining propagation to other observers; it is not a claim of zero physical propagation time.

before.definition: Independent Reads of Independent Writes: two writers update different words and two readers read them in opposite orders. With each reader’s loads suitably ordered, opposite observations of write order are forbidden by the stated multicopy-atomic hardware model; unordered readers or language acquire mappings require separate analysis.

after.definition: Independent Reads of Independent Writes: two writers update different words and two readers read them in opposite orders. With each reader’s loads suitably ordered, opposite observations of write order are forbidden by the stated multicopy-atomic hardware model; unordered readers or language acquire mappings require separate analysis.

before.definition: A machine-level test where one thread writes data then a flag and another reads the flag then data. With the lesson’s ordinary aligned coherent memory assumptions, x86-TSO forbids seeing the new flag with old data; Arm needs suitable ordering. Unsynchronised C/C++ ordinary objects would instead cause a data race.

after.definition: A machine-level test where one thread writes data then a flag and another reads the flag then data. With the lesson’s ordinary aligned coherent memory assumptions, x86-TSO forbids seeing the new flag with old data; Arm needs suitable ordering. Unsynchronised C/C++ ordinary objects would instead cause a data race.

before.definition: In the C/C++ memory model, the link created when an acquire operation reads the value written by a release operation. It makes the releasing thread's earlier writes visible to the acquiring thread.

after.definition: A C/C++ synchronisation relation. For the atomic publication pattern here, a release operation synchronises with an acquire operation that reads from its release sequence, making relevant earlier work happen before the acquiring thread’s later work. Other synchronisation operations have their own rules.

before.definition: Data-race-free implies sequentially consistent: the guarantee that a program with no data races, using only locks and seq_cst atomics, behaves as if sequentially consistent.

after.definition: The sequential-consistency guarantee for a data-race-free program using mutexes and seq_cst atomic operations without weaker synchronisation operations. Being data-race-free alone does not make a program using weaker atomics sequentially consistent.

before.definition: A classic lock for two threads using only loads and stores of two flags and a turn variable. It is correct under sequential consistency but needs a fence on x86 because of store-to-load reordering.

after.definition: A two-participant mutual-exclusion algorithm using flags and a turn variable. The standard algorithm is correct under sequential consistency; ordinary x86-TSO assembly needs suitable store-before-load ordering, such as correctly placed full fences. A C/C++ implementation must additionally obey language atomicity and ordering rules.

before.definition: A CUDA grouping of thread blocks guaranteed to run at the same time on neighbouring SMs, so they can synchronise and share memory. Available on newer GPUs.

after.definition: A supported CUDA grouping of thread blocks guaranteed to be co-scheduled within one GPU Processing Cluster (GPC). It enables explicit cluster synchronisation and distributed shared-memory access under documented participation and lifetime rules; physical adjacency of individual SMs is not the contract.

before.definition: One logical thread of a GPU kernel, with its own registers and indices. Thousands run at once; the hardware issues their instructions a warp of 32 at a time.

after.definition: One logical CUDA kernel thread with its own execution state and block/thread indices. A launch may expose thousands of threads; hardware groups consecutive linear block-thread indices into warps and issues instructions to active participants subject to resource limits.

before.definition: When active threads of a warp choose different control-flow paths. A simplified masked-path model executes the paths separately; actual scheduling, predication and elapsed cost depend on the code and target, so path times do not universally add exactly.
before.example: An if taking 100 cycles and an else taking 60 cost a divergent warp about 160.

after.definition: When active threads of a warp choose different control-flow paths. A simplified masked-path model executes the paths separately; actual scheduling, predication and elapsed cost depend on the code and target, so path times do not universally add exactly.
after.example: In a stated no-overlap masked-path model, paths costing 100 and 60 cycles take about 160 cycles together; actual device timing requires measurement.

before.definition: A grid of simple processing elements that each multiply, add and pass values to their neighbours every clock cycle, so each operand fetched is reused many times as it flows through. The name compares the rhythmic data flow to a heartbeat.

after.definition: An array of processing elements with a regular, rhythmic local dataflow, often forwarding operands or partial results between neighbours. A matrix-multiply design can reuse operands across many multiply-accumulate operations; the precise operation, dataflow and busy cycles depend on the design.

before.definition: One cell of a systolic array or similar accelerator: a small unit that multiplies, accumulates and forwards data to its neighbours.

after.definition: A computing cell in a parallel array. In this module’s matrix-array model, each cell multiplies a pair of operands, accumulates a result and participates in the stated neighbour dataflow; other arrays may use different operations.

before.definition: The fraction of available hardware capacity doing useful work over a period.

after.definition: The fraction of a stated hardware resource capacity used for the chosen work. State the denominator: useful processing-element cycles, active lane capacity and requested memory-sector bytes are different measurements and must not be treated as interchangeable.

before.definition: Sending part of a computation from the host CPU to an accelerator. It pays only if the time saved exceeds data transfer and setup costs.

after.definition: Sending part of a computation from a host processor to an accelerator. To reduce elapsed time, the saved computation must outweigh added transfers, setup and synchronisation after accounting for any valid overlap; energy and throughput objectives need their own comparisons.

before.definition: Top-down category for slots used by micro-operations that completed and were kept.

after.definition: Top-down category for slots used by micro-operations that completed and were kept.

before.definition: Top-down category for slots lost because execution resources or memory were not ready. It splits into memory bound and core bound.

after.definition: Intel top-down category attributing slots to backend resource pressure, such as execution resources or the memory subsystem. It is refined into core-bound and memory-bound categories under processor-specific metrics; the percentage is not directly an elapsed-time fraction.

before.definition: Short for floating point, as in FP32 or FP reduction semantics.

after.definition: Short for floating point, as in FP32 or FP reduction semantics.

before.definition: Changing how operations are grouped. Exact integer arithmetic is associative; fixed-width unsigned addition wraps modulo its width, while signed C overflow is undefined. Floating-point regrouping can change rounding, overflow and cancellation results.
before.example: In float32, first cancelling equal large opposite values and then adding one can differ from first adding one to one of the large values.

after.definition: Changing how operations are grouped. Mathematical integer addition and multiplication are associative; fixed-width unsigned addition wraps modulo its width, while signed C overflow is undefined. Floating-point regrouping can change rounding, overflow and cancellation results.
after.example: In float32, first cancelling equal large opposite values and then adding one can differ from first adding one to one of the large values.

after.definition: Useful bytes requested by participating threads divided by the bytes covered by the requested GPU memory sectors. This is a byte-footprint ratio, distinct from the fraction of time an execution unit is busy; caches can make actual DRAM traffic different.

corrections.reason: Separate byte-footprint utilisation and top-down subcategories from broader parent concepts.

after.definition: The Intel top-down backend subcategory for execution-core resource pressure rather than the memory-bound subcategory. The exact metrics depend on the processor; its slot share is not directly elapsed time.

corrections.reason: Separate byte-footprint utilisation and top-down subcategories from broader parent concepts.

after.definition: Slots attributed to memory-related backend pressure in the selected Intel top-down metrics. This can include several memory-system constraints and is not automatically a fraction of elapsed time spent waiting for loads.

corrections.reason: Separate byte-footprint utilisation and top-down subcategories from broader parent concepts.

before.definition: Compiler options (such as GCC and Clang -ffast-math) that relax strict IEEE floating-point rules: allowing reassociation, ignoring NaN and infinity cases, and more. They can speed code up and also change or break numerical results.

after.definition: Compiler options (such as GCC and Clang -ffast-math) that relax strict IEEE floating-point rules: allowing reassociation, ignoring NaN and infinity cases, and more. They can speed code up and also change or break numerical results.

before.definition: GCC and Clang options that choose which CPU's instruction set the compiler may use. -march=native targets the build machine, so the binary may crash with SIGILL on older CPUs.

after.definition: GCC and Clang target options that permit particular instruction sets or processor features. A -march CPU target can enable several extensions, while -mavx2 enables AVX2; -march=native targets the build machine and can make a binary incompatible with older deployment CPUs.

before.definition: Adjusting a machine-learning model’s parameters from data. Numerical formats and accumulation requirements depend on the algorithm and implementation; bfloat16, float32 and other formats may be combined.

after.definition: Adjusting a machine-learning model’s parameters from data. Numerical formats and accumulation requirements depend on the algorithm and implementation; bfloat16, float32 and other formats may be combined.

before.definition: Using different floating-point formats in one computation, for example bfloat16 multiplies with float32 accumulation.

after.definition: Using different floating-point formats in one computation, for example bfloat16 multiplies with float32 accumulation.

before.definition: Intel's 2013 CPU microarchitecture, Intel's first to support AVX2 and FMA; the CPU comparison in the 2017 TPU paper.

after.definition: An Intel CPU microarchitecture supporting AVX2 and FMA. Haswell-based CPUs were the CPU comparison in the 2017 first-TPU paper; actual throughput depends on the selected processor and workload.

before.definition: An NVIDIA data-centre GPU from 2014 used as the GPU comparison in the 2017 TPU paper.

after.definition: An NVIDIA data-centre GPU family used for the GPU comparison in the 2017 first-TPU paper. The paper’s compared system and workload are required context for its performance ratios.

corrections.reason: Give the specific reassociation option its own contract rather than treating it as the full fast-math option bundle.

before.definition: Top-down category for slots spent on work that was thrown away, mostly after branch mispredictions.

after.definition: Intel top-down category for slots lost to incorrect speculation, including issued micro-operations that do not retire and slots blocked during recovery. Branch mispredictions and machine clears can contribute; the exact metric is processor-specific.

corrections.reason: Include recovery slots as well as discarded issued work, matching Intel Appendix B.1.6.
